newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa's Griquas say rights struggle goes on.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Griquas say rights struggle goes on.

text.p: South Africa's Griqua community on Thursday welcomed a government decision to recognise them officially as a separate ethnic group, but said their struggle for land and other rights was far from over.
The Griquas trace their roots to marriages in the second half of the 18th Century between indigenous Bushmen and European settlers moving into the interior from the Cape.
They object to being classified as Coloureds, the South African term for the descendants of liaisons between whites and blacks.
"This was just a first step," Cecil le Fleur, chairman of the Griqua National Conference, said in an interview. "There's still a long battle to fight."

Constitutional Development Minister Mohammed Valli Moosa said on Tuesday after a meeting with le Fleur and other Griqua leaders that the government of President Nelson Mandela would for the first time recognise them as an ethnic community in their own right.
But le Fleur said this recognition needed to be incorporated in the constitution and needed to go further to recognise the Griquas as an indigenous "first nation" like the Aborigines of Australia.

Le Fleur said Mandela's government had granted the Griquas recognition only after the Griqua National Conference exerted pressure, including taking their case to a U.N. workshop on "first nations" in Geneva.
He said the Griquas would press for restitution of land he believed was wrongly taken from them by the British colonial government and De Beers Consolidated Mines in the last century.
The land includes farms and diamond mining areas in the Northern Cape and Free State provinces.

"I want to stress that we are not asking for a volkstaat," le Fleur said, referring to the "people's state" which right-wing white Afrikaners want as a territory where they can rule themselves. "We will press our land claims in a responsible way."
